units.title: Why is it harder to learn a second language?
paragraphs: Good morning, everyone. In our last lecture, we discussed briefly first language acquisition. We have learned that we are born to process and produce natural human language by looking at what we are exposed to, or what we create with the universal grammar principles that we are born with. [We also know that we acquire our native language in a natural way. However, if you have had the experience of trying to master a second language, no doubt you find it to be a challenge, uh, quite unlike your first language experience. Because there are important differences between acquiring a first language and learning a second one. So in today’s lecture, I will discuss why it is harder to learn a second language by comparing the differences and
similarities between these two ways of language processing: And I’ll finish by briefly mentioning a related topic, that is language translation.

Now let’s come to the differences first. First of all, as everybody knows, anyone who is learning a second language has already acquired a first language, right? So the language mechanism in the brain has already had certain linguistic parameters set, such as word order in the first language, Jand that makes
second language learning quite different. What one needs to learn are the specific rules of the second

language, which is often called the target language. In second language learning, the first language tends to serve as a model, and mistakes often result from taking words from the target language and putting them together, because learners tend to apply rules from the first language. For example, if the first language is English and the target language is Korean, a second-language learner might position the Korean verb between the subject and the object of the sentence, using the English word order, rather than placing the verb after the object, which is the correct Korean word order. Generally speaking, the greater the difference between the first language and the target language, the more tasks are involved in learning the latter. What’s more, second language learning can even be characterized as a gradual shift from the first language orientation to the target language orientation.

OK, let’s come to the second point. As we all know, first language acquisition typically takes place in early childhood, at a very young age. However, second language learning, especially in a classroom setting, proceeds more quickly with adults and adolescence than with younger children initially, although at the end of the day, it is the younger child who will become more proficient in second language learning than ,
grownups. That is to say, even in second language learning, age is also a major factor, as in first language
acquisition. ， The third point I want to bring up here is that it’s apparent that first language acquisition happens
without conscious teaching, you know, in a kind of natural way, as I mentioned just now. But the second
language learning generally does not. Numerous studies have shown that /a number of traits, such as
self-confidence, motivation, good self-image and low anxiety, can facilitate second language learning, but none of these traits seem as important to first language acquisition.

OK, let’s move to the fourth point. Studies have shown that the input that affects second language learning is more complex than that in a first language acquisition context. What do I mean here? Now, let me

give you an example. If a second language learner has a classroom teacher who talks in the target language at a quick rate, in complex sentences and about complicated matters, the learner will probably have a harder time in the learning process. However, first language acquisition can proceed at the same rate, whether or not adults simplify their language.

Now, the fifth point is that practice is important for second language learning, but not so much for first language acquisition. Even very quiet children, I mean, kids who don’t like to talk to people, can acquire their first language at the ordinary rate, but that doesn’t work for a second language learner. For example, he
or she has to constantly practice listening and speaking in order to be proficient in that language. This means that second language learners need to put in a lot more effort.

Despite the differences I’ve mentioned between first language ‘acquisition and second language learning, they also share a few similarities. Let’s take a look at them. First is the learning speed. Second language learning can proceed as quickly as first language acquisition if the target language is used as the medium of instruction. Then the next is language exposure, which is both important in the two processes. As in first language acquisition, second language learning can be more successful when richly interactive language is used in the classroom. That’ is, exposure to authentic language, be it oral or written, is a better teaching strategy than memorization drills or recitations.

So far, I’ve taken you through some of the differences and similarities between first language acquisition and second language learning. [14)You may find second language learning is, to some extent, a much harder

process than first language acquisition. A final point here, which is closely related to second language learning, that is a language translation. In language learning classes, you are often asked to translate between languages as a form of exercise or assessment, and you may have already faced challenges when transforming one language into the other. There is an Italian saying which goes something like this: “Translators, traitors.” What it really means is that translation can never be perfect, so anyone who translates necessarily betrays the original, more or less. In my opinion, translation is not a mechanical act. Rather, translation is a creative

act. Some have even said that translating is rewriting. Different translators will offer different translations of the same text. And these different translations have their own strengths and drawbacks. So in my next lecture, we’ll discuss the complexity of language translation. Thank you.

units.title: Interview 1
paragraphs: Hello, Barry, nice to have you on our program.
Thanks.

Now, you’ve enjoyed a very successful career as one of the leading public intellectuals and commentators on current and global events, and also as one of the most distinguished contemporary novelists. What do you think of your two activities?

Well, since I have two brains, I have two ways of writing. That is, literary creation and critical writing. T like them equally well. This, as a matter of fact, allows for a rotation, which lets one brain rest while the other one works.
: OK, then which of the two activities, fiction or essay writing, do you find more demanding, and more
satisfying?
: Well, everything is difficult in the writing of a book, whether it. is fiction or theory. But, I’'d say
writing fiction is probably more arduous because you have to create a completely new world, and not just comment on an existing one. It offers a complete universe which holds your interest throughout
the novel and hopefully will leave a lasting impression. So I wonder if a good novel doesn’t endure
longer than an essay, because the essay is limited to the time in which it is written. In any case,

producing both of these at once is an aesthetic risk because you can be disowned by both camps. Your work can be considered not serious enough for the philosophers and too theoretical for the novelists. But I like generating new things in this way.
: Hmm. Now let’s focus on fiction writing. From your point of view, are there any themes and subjects
that are... are particularly appropriate to fiction writing? ©
: Well, I’d like to say novels and essays treat similar themes but from a different viewpoint. For

me, novel writing is characterized by a search for extremes. It is always an attempt to escape from oneself, from the conventions, from professional and familial success. We only write well in the grip of emotion, and the novel speaks a truth that would be inaudible in an essay. And then the essay. It leads back to the idea of reality, but the novel frees us from it. It expresses an urge toward disorder, toward , fantasy which goes beyond normal limits.
: OK. You write with great clarity in your novels. If you were to single out novels, which ones do you
find especially inspirational or compelling?

It’s only through clarity that we achieve depth in fiction writing. I am attracted to very different genres, for example, the magic realism of South America, the literature of ancient China and Central Europe, the Gothic novels, and certain works of science fiction, and it is often minor novels which
have impressed me the longest. Barry, Another question for you. Given our increasingly visual and “mediatized” culture, how do you
see the future of fiction writing?

M: Our country remains one of those rare countries where people still buy lots of books, many more than elsewhere. So it’s a marvelous place for writers. As a result, novels proliferate here just like rabbits. Everyone wants to write. Literature isn’t threatened by becoming a rarity but rather by obesity.
: Excuse me, what do you mean by obesity?

Well, we’re reaching a situation in which there are more writers than readers. 700 novels were published in September last year, and 500 in January this year. This has caused the public to turn away . in confusion. But let’s not complain about this excess of books. The point is, how can we find our way around? I think there are still a. few alternatives, for example, to stick to the classics, to follow
the list of best-sellers of the moment, or to collect a private library of books, one that you share with special friends. Actually, we usually mix these three alternatives.
W: Thank you very much, Barry, for coming to talk on our program.
M: Pleasure.

units.title: Interview 2
paragraphs: ' W: Antarctica, a continent of snow and ice, is now losing ice three times faster than it was in 2007. In a

new study published last week in the journal Nature, more than 80 scientists from multiple countries used satellite data to examine the Antarctica’s vast ice sheets, and their prediction is that if the
current rate of ice melt continues, sea levels could rise six inches by the year 2100. Joining us today

for more on this study and the consequences of sea level rise is Benjamin Johnson, president and CEO of Climate Watch. So Ben, we’ve heard about sea level rise for years. How significant is this particular study and what did it look at?

M: Well, the first thing I’d like to point out is Antarctica is just one part of the story. That is to say, we have six inches of contribution from. Antarctica if it continues to shed ice at the rate it was measured. But, but there are other sources as well. So all together, we would be looking at three feet.
W: M
: Three feet of sea level risé by the year 2100. That is consequential to hundreds of millions of people that live in coastal cities all over the planet.

: Yes, it is. We’re already seeing floods increase. Yesterday, for example, there were huge floods at some of the areas around the country, and these floods wouldn’t have happened without the sea level rise that we’ve already seen.
: Yeah, and what is it that is convincing these scientists that the rates are changing? What are they studying? What are they looking at? How can they tell?
: Well, they have a lot of direct measurements from satellites of the height of the surface of the ice
sheets, so they’re able to see how that height changes over time. These satellites also measure the
gravitational pull of the ice sheet and, and therefore the scientists know how much ice is there. So those are the two main forms of measurement.
:I knew that there are climate science deniers who say “look at the east side of Antarctica, it looks on a map, there’s actually more ice coming in.” Doesn’t this all balance itself out?
: We do anticipate that in the future, snowfall will increase in East Antarctica and I hope so. But this
study shows over recent decades it hasn’t.
: Does it mean that if nothing is going to change, areas around on coastal waterways will be severely
impacted?
: Yeah. If we continue to see the ice melt speeding up, and don’t cut back on our climate pollution
emissions, then we’re pointed more toward six feet, possibly, rather than the three feet predicted by 2100, and that will be unmanageable in very many places. ,

: Also the effects that we’re seeing of sea level rise, of climate change in a global capacity. This is because of the carbon that we’ve already put into the atmosphere, not just exactly what we’re doing today. So even if everyone stopped driving, all the factories shut down, and somehow we didn’t produce CO2, we’re still going to see the effects of climate change.
: Yes, we are. Unfortunately, once the carbon is in the atmosphere, most of it stays for hundreds and
thousands of years. But if we do something to control our pollution NOW, we can really slow it down a lot and make it more manageable, and that’s the name of the game, really. Slower change will
be much more manageable than the fast change. That is possible. All right, Ben. Thank you so much for talking to us. : Pleasure.
